newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UAE urges Iran to scrap plant on disputed islands.
newsitem.headline: UAE urges Iran to scrap plant on disputed islands.

text.p: The United Arab Emirates (UAE) called on Iran on Tuesday to dismantle installations that it said had been built on three disputed Gulf islands and to enter into negotiations for a settlement or refer the issue to the world court.

"Twenty-five years have passed since the occupation by the Islamic Republic of Iran of our three islands: Greater Tunb, Lesser Tunb and Abu Moussa," UAE Foreign Minister Rashid Abdullah al-Nuaimi said in a speech to the General Assembly.
"These are Arab islands, Arab in their history and origin," he said. "They are the pillars of our national sovereignty, territorial integrity and overall inalienable national rights."
Nuaimi said Iran rejected peaceful endeavours aimed at resolving the problem and "established and equipped facilities whose features are not exclusively civil."

He said an electrical power plant had been built on Greater Tunb; and an airport, refrigeration plant and fish-processing plant on Abu Moussa, while Iranian nationals, mostly from the military, had been settled on the islands.

"We view this as a clear act of provocation aiming at changing the demographic character of the islands and imposing a new fait accompli. By doing so, Iran has consecrated its illegitimate occupation," Nuaimi said.

Iran failed to heed repeated appeals by the UAE, the Gulf Cooperation Council, the last Arab summit meeting and the council of the Arab League, he said, adding that this was not only a violation of his country's sovereignty but also of international law.
"We therefore call upon the government of Iran to dismantle all the illegitimately established civil and military facilities on our three islands," Nuaimi said.

"We also call upon it to respond to the peace initiatives advanced and supported by the sisterly and friendly peace-loving countries, and to enter into unconditional bilateral negotiations conducive to a peaceful settlement of the dispute, or to refer the case to the International Court of Justice."

At the end of the day an Iranian representative, Ali Abolhassani Shahreza, exercised his right of reply to say the UAE minister had leveled "a number of baseless allegations and raised unacceptable claims against the territorial integrity" of Iran which had no historical or legal foundations.
He did not see "any genuine utility for a rhetorical approach to this issue," whether in the General Assembly or elsewhere.

"We are confident that the existing misundertandings will be resolved in our bilateral talks and in a neighbourly atmosphere," he said, welcoming the UAE's readiness to engage in bilateral discussions without preconditions by either side.

In response the UAE's U.N. ambassador, Mohammad Samhan, said that when the issue was discussed last year Iran "insisted on raising secondary issues unrelated to the question, thus showing a lack of seriousness" and lack of readiness to settle the issue on a bilateral level.
He asked how the islands could be Iranian when he said the Iranian government had tried to purchase or rent them as far back as 1922, finally occupying them in 1971.

In the past few years an attempt had been made to "promote and strengthen military control over the three islands, including the stockpiling of weapons of mass destruction and entrenching the occupation of the three islands," he said.
